item.title: Jetten says it is “not his place” to join Gaza demonstration
item.description:
Jetten says it is “not his place” to join Gaza demonstration

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten has defended his decision to stay away from last weekend’s mass demonstration in Amsterdam against Israel’s war in Gaza.

Organisers claimed around 200,000 people joined the Red Line rally, the fourth to be held since Israel began its bombing campaign and ground offensive in response to the attacks by Hamas in October 2023.

Jetten took part in a similar demonstration in Amsterdam in October last year as leader of the D66 party, which was then in opposition, but said it was “not his place” to attend as prime minister. He also declined to describe Israel’s offensive as a genocide, as he did a year ago.

“Hundreds of thousands of people in the Netherlands took to the streets because they are concerned about the terrible humanitarian situation of many Palestinians,” he said.

“That’s why the cabinet has pledged from the outset to offer more help and put pressure on Israel.”

But he added: “I don’t think it’s my place at all to be at a demonstration like this. People have shown how moved they are by the situation of millions of Palestinians and at the same time they have urged the cabinet to act.”

VVD blockade

The prime minister has come under pressure from human rights organisations to speak out against Israel, but his coalition includes the right-wing liberal VVD party, whose leadership is staunchly pro-Israeli.

Jetten insisted at his weekly press conference on Friday that the Dutch government had made clear during bilateral talks with Israel that “the situation in Gaza, the West Bank, but also in Jordan and Syria is unacceptable”.

But he ruled out taking stronger measures such as an arms embargo or declaring that Israel was committing “genocide and ethnic cleansing against Palestinians”, as the protest organisers demanded.

Senior politicians including Amsterdam’s former Labour party (PvdA) mayor Job Cohen have also criticised Jetten’s leadership on the issue.

Cohen and former VVD foreign affairs minister, Jozias van Aartsen, who are both Jewish, said in an interview with the Volkskrant at the weekend that they were joining the demonstration to protest against Israel’s actions.

Humanitarian values

Cohen told TV talks show Pauw, De Wit and Moggré: “I have had doubts in the past, specifically about the term genocide, because I found it so incredibly difficult to apply it not to Israel, but to this Israeli government.

“I think it’s extremely important that Israel exists as a place of refuge where Jews can go, but I think this government is appalling. My feeling is that it’s almost impossible to deny anymore that what is happening, to an increasing degree, has elements of genocide.”

Van Aartsen was critical of his own party for refusing to push for sanctions against Israel. “It would be fitting for a party that claims to be liberal to defend basic values such as humanity and international law, but they are standing by and watching,” he said.

item.title: Tilburg arms manufacturer buys rights to Israeli weapon designs
item.description:
Tilburg arms manufacturer buys rights to Israeli weapon designs

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Tilburg-based defence company AIA is buying technological data from Israeli arms manufacturer IWI, best known for the Uzi machine gun, and which is the main supplier of small arms for the Israeli military and police forces, broadcaster NOS reported.

AIA is specifically buying design information for two guns, noted for their ability to shoot down drones, the Arad 5 rifle and the Negev UX light machine gun.

AIA’s director Gerard Zondervan told NOS that “Europe is calling”, that the bloc needs to produce its own weapons, and that he would not discuss politically contentious issues regarding Israel such as the war on Gaza.

In January, MPs adopted a motion calling on the government to reduce the Netherlands’ reliance on Israeli weapons, citing concerns about war crimes. The motion says the Netherlands has bought €2 billion worth of equipment from Israeli defence firms in recent years.

The Netherlands has also blocked exports of F-35 fighter jet parts to Israel since an appeals court ruling in February 2024, and kept the ban in place after the Supreme Court overturned that ruling in October 2025.

Zondervan said AIA had had no contact with the Dutch government regarding the deal, and that production will begin in Tilburg and then move into an expanded facility in Overijssel.

The announcement comes shortly after the defence ministry launched the National Institute for Defence technology (NIDT), to speed up development and cooperation for the arms industry.

NIDT will get €350 million a year from 2028 onwards, intended to strengthen defences in the North Sea amid escalating conflict with Russia.

item.title: Parents spending more on private lessons to boost exam chances
item.description:
Parents spending more on private lessons to boost exam chances

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Parents are booking extra home school lessons in the last years of primary school to boost their children’s performance in tests and improve their chances of being accepted for the top tier of secondary schools.

Official government figures show that the amount households spent on help with homework, out-of-school lessons and exam training more than tripled in the 10 years from €151 million to €472 million.

Support for primary school children accounted for €44 million of the total, but education specialist told the Volkskrant that the strongest growth was in help for children in groups 6, 7 and 8 of primary school.

Dutch children are streamed when they enter secondary school, from vwo level, which prepares children for university, down to vmbo and praktijkonderwijs, which focus on practical skills.

Sezgin Cihangir, director of the Mathematisch Instituut in Amstelveen, said many parents were paying for extra lessons to compensate for the poor quality of school education.

His institution, which charges €1,790 for a 12-week course of extra maths tuition, claims on its website to have improved the Cito test scores for 92% of children who take part.

“For us it’s about improving children’s basic skills so that they can go through school with more self-reliance and self-confidence,” he said. “What we do isn’t extra tuition, it’s damage limitation.”

Inequality

Louise Elffers, professor of equality in education at the University of Amsterdam, said the growth of out-of-school tuition favoured families who could afford to pay for the lessons.

“Research has shown that the educational level of parents is a bigger factor in choosing to send children for extra lessons than their income, but well-educated people often earn more as well,” she said.

“Parents want their child to achieve the best possible diploma so they can get further up the hierarchy. Well-educated parents are especially conscious of this and investing more in their children’s school careers.”

But Cihangir said parents on all income levels were prepared to pay extra to improve their children’s chances.

“I’ve had people here who live on welfare,” he said. “If parents see that their child needs it, they make sure they can find a way to afford it.”

item.title: Dutch state collecting too much data on activists, report says
item.description:
Dutch state collecting too much data on activists, report says

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch institute for human rights says it is concerned about how much information the government is collecting on political activists, and fears an expansion in technological and legal powers by state forces could suppress protests in the future.

In its annual report, the institute looked at the different ways local authorities collect information on protestors. Legally, it says, people only need to notify that demonstration will take place – not get permission. And they can do that anonymously, the report says.

But several local authorities ask for personal information from people when they register a protest notification. Institute chair Rick Lawson told broadcaster NOS that organisers are asked for their name, where they live, whether they have social media accounts, who they expect to attend and what message they want to put across.

That information can help councils and police make sure a protest runs smoothly and assess the risk of counter-protests or disorder, Lawson said. “That is understandable, but it leads to distrust.”

A specialist unit in the Dutch police called TOOI researches people through social media and other sources before a protest goes ahead to prevent potential threats. Police also gather information from citizen informants and officers on the street. The institute wants these powers limited to what can be legally justified in every case.

The use of cameras at demonstrations is a case in point. They can be used for facial recognition at protests under strict circumstances but never in real-time. What data is collected and how long it actually stored in reality is a threat that could deter lawful protesting, the institute says.

Three new bills seeking to expand data collection powers are currently in the works, which the institute stresses are not necessary. It says 97% of protests go ahead without incidents, and only 0.03% ever record more than 10 incidents.

The institute is calling on the government to be cautious about implementing new powers, to collect as little personal data as possible on notification forms and make clear that organisers can notify anonymously, and to tell people what information is held on them and what rights they have.

The report follows a year of frequent protesting, often over the influx of asylum seekers. Mass protests against the war on Gaza have also been held four times this year and last.

item.title: Housing minister plans new village at Netherlands’ lowest point
item.description:
Housing minister plans new village at Netherlands’ lowest point

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The government is pressing ahead with plans to build a new village of 6,000 homes at the lowest point in the Netherlands, more than six metres below sea level.

The construction of Cortelande, in the Zuidplaspolder near Gouda, is one of five projects named by housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan in the latest stage of her national plan to build more than 400,000 new homes by 2040.

The €132 million project, originally announced by O’Sullivan’s predecessor Mona Keijzer, led to a legal row between the local council and the local water board, but the latter withdrew its appeal in July after talks to safeguard the water supplies.

Experts have warned that building the village, which lies 6.78m below NAP, the baseline used to determine elevation in the Netherlands, will be especially challenging.

“We’re pushing the boundaries,” researcher Floris Boogaard of hydraulic engineering research specialist Delatres told NOS. “The ground might rise here, but you’re building on soft ground, especially when it’s so deep. We’ve never built so deep before on such a large scale.”

The other four projects named by Boekholt-O’Sullivan are in Assen, Drenthe, where up to 6,000 homes will be built in three suburbs, another 3,500 houses in Best, Noord-Brabant, up to 6,000 homes in Roosendaal, a key rail hub on the Belgian border, and 5,000 homes in the Zeeland towns of Middleburg, Vlissingen and Veere.

item.title: Dutch home workers reluctant to spend more time in the office
item.description:
Dutch home workers reluctant to spend more time in the office

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More than half of people who work from home would struggle to return to the office full-time because their home and working lives have become so intertwined, according to a survey for the FNV union and current affairs show Nieuwsuur.

The most common reasons for the 3,000 workers not to increase their office hours were concerns about declining productivity, more time spent commuting and a negative impact on their health and well-being.

Businesses have tried to encourage their staff to spend more time in the office since the end of the coronavirus pandemic, but none of the Netherlands’ 25 largest companies said they require their employees to leave the house five days a week.

Jelle Kajim, who works for HR support company Remote, told Nieuwsuur he valued the flexibility of working from home.

“We have 2,000 people, but we don’t have any offices,” he said. “In 10 years I’ve never worked in an office and sometimes I’m curious about it.

“I recently had to go to Paris for work, but I don’t see myself sitting in a metro train every day.”

Booking.com case

Travel website Booking.com won a court case last month against its works council, which objected to the company’s plans to compel staff to spend 40% of their contracted hours at its head office in Amsterdam.

The judge in the case remarked that it was “very normal” for people to travel to work two days a week, but only around a quarter of the company’s staff currently do so.

Other major employers said they had embraced the concept of homeworking in recent years. Just 14% of new collective bargaining agreements in 2019 made arrangements for working from home, but last year the proportion rose to 38%.

A spokesman for insurer Nationale Nederlanden said it promoted a balanced approach, with staff encouraged to spend two days a week in the office.

“The strength of working in the office lies mainly in co-operation, innovation, development and social conections. The strength of home working lies in flexibility, concentration and a good balance between work and private life,” a spokesman said.

Rabobank, which does not have a minimum office-time requirement, said: “We see no reason to set a target for presenteeism. Our experiences with hybrid working are positive.”

item.title: Foreign workers often left in the dark over EU pension rights
item.description:
Foreign workers often left in the dark over EU pension rights

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

People in the Netherlands who have worked in multiple EU countries have no way of knowing how much pension they’ve built up, and the country is not yet part of a European system to fix the problem, according to broadcaster NOS.

There is no single body covering all EU member states, so if you lived and worked in other countries for some time you have to remember to contact each one before retiring.

“It is incredibly complicated,” Lisa Bruggen, director of pension research institute Netspar, told NOS. You can’t simply add up the amounts you see on, for example, the Dutch and German pension portals, because they’re calculated differently.

Around 700,000 people receiving the Dutch state pension (AOW) currently get a reduced amount because they lived abroad, according to social insurance bank SVB.

Foreign workers in lower-paid sectors such as construction, hospitality and transport are most at risk of pension poverty, NOS said.

One pension fund told the broadcaster it has some 18,000 retired members who have not claimed their pension, but that privacy rules prevent it from tracing them.

An EU-backed platform, Find Your Pension, aims to show people where they have pension savings, how much they are worth, and how to claim them. The Dutch pension law must be changed before the Netherlands can join, the social affairs ministry told NOS, saying that the cabinet is working on it.

The organisation behind the platform does not expect the Netherlands to join before 2028. Even after more than a decade of work, the platform can so far retrieve personal pension information only from Belgium and France, and users say that does not always work.

item.title: Work exhaustion rising, especially among women and young people
item.description:
Work exhaustion rising, especially among women and young people

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Exhaustion from work has been on the rise in the Netherlands for the past decade, with 21% of people saying they feel mentally fatigued at least a few times per month, according to new research by national statistics office CBS and research institute TNO. In 2015, the figure was 13%.

The findings are drawn from an annual national survey of around 57,000 people aged 15 to 74, excluding self employed. Mental fatigue was defined as feeling mentally exhausted several times per month at least, for example feeling emotionally drained or empty at the end of the day.

Women are more affected than men, the survey showed. In 2025, 24% of female employees reported fatigue, up from 14% a decade earlier. Among men, the figure rose from 13% to 18%.

Younger people are the most affected, with the 25-34 year-old age group showing the biggest rise. In 2015, 15% reported fatigue and in 2025 the number had risen to 28%. In 2023, TNO found that one in four workers aged 18 to 34 had burnout complaints.

The more complex the job, the higher the chance of mental fatigue. People in the most complex jobs, which involve highly specialised tasks and usually require a higher level of education, had a fatigue rate of 23%, compared with 18% in the least complex jobs.

Psychologists and sociologists reported the highest rate of fatigue, at 37%. The least exhausted were those working in agriculture, at only 12%.

Psychological complaints, stress and burnout were the reason for 9% of employees’ most recent sick leave, second only to flu and colds (55%). They also kept people off work the longest, at an average of 67 days, compared with 15 days for sick leave overall.

Burnout was also the most commonly reported occupational illness, with 1.9% of workers saying a doctor had diagnosed them with burnout or work-related stress. In July 2025, psychiatrists and occupational health experts called for a rethink of burnout diagnosis in the Netherlands, after Sweden dropped the term.

Two months later, the government’s health advisory council RVS warned of a “hypernervous society”, estimating the cost of mental health problems at €18 billion a year.

item.title: PSV back on top of Eredivisie as Feyenoord slump in Heerenveen
item.description:
PSV back on top of Eredivisie as Feyenoord slump in Heerenveen

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

PSV returned to the top of the Eredivisie with a thumping 5-2 win over Cambuur Leeuwarden as previous leaders Feyenoord lost a seven-goal thriller against the other Frisian club, Heerenveen.

It took just 46 seconds for PSV to get off the mark as Sven Mijnans headed in unmarked.

The midfielder added a second after 15 minutes and completed his hat-trick with a free-kick in the 80th minute to make the score 4-2, just as Cambuur were threatening a comeback.

Feyenoord’s dip in form continued as they let a two-goal lead slip at Heerenveen. The Rotterdammers looked to be in control going into the break with a trademark drilled shot by Anis Hadj Moussa and a penalty by Nacho Ferri.

But Maas Willemsen bundled in the ball from a corner on the stroke of half-time, before Ringo Meerveld came on for the second half and scored a hat-trick as Feyenoord’s defence crumbled under pressure.

“In the matches when we played well I saw a team that fought for each other,” Feyenoord coach Giovanni van Bronckhorst said after the game. “Mentally strong, kept running even when we didn’t have the ball. That’s our strength. When we don’t do that we’re a lesser team.”

Meerdinck penalty drama

Mexx Meerdink scored a hotly contested late penalty to settle a tempestuous game in Alkmaar as AZ came back from 3-1 down against Groningen to claim their first win in five matches.

Goalkeeper Etienne Vaessen was given a second yellow card for protesting too hard against the decision to penalise him for upending Ayoub Oufkir. Once the commotion died down Meerdink, who had missed from the spot against Vaessen earlier in the second half, made no mistake against substitute goalkeeper Lovro Stubljar.

Ajax missed the chance to take over top spot at Twente as their former striker Wout Weghorst scored a last-minute penalty to rescue a point for the home side.

Ajax had been 2-0 up with a bullet header by their giant striker Tolu Arokodare and a long-range strike by Rayane Bounida, before an own goal by Dies Janse brought the visitors back into the game.

Valk own goal

Fortuna Sittard also had to settle for a point against Telstar after going 2-0 up thanks to a bizarre own goal by Sem Valk. The defender’s sliced clearance looped over the head of Ronald Koeman Junior as the goalkeeper tried to head it away rather than risk being penalised for handling a backpass.

Goals just before half-time by Abdelnour Soualhia and Patrick Brouwer brought Telstar back into the game, but neither side was able to find a winner after the break.

That result allowed ADO, under the guidance of interim coach Levi Schwiebbe, to close the gap on 16th-placed Telstar to one point with a 3-1 win against Sparta, while bottom Willem II collected their third point of the season at home to PEC Zwolle.

item.title: Fog warning issued as mist engulfs north-east Netherlands
item.description:
Fog warning issued as mist engulfs north-east Netherlands

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A code yellow weather warning has been issued by the KNMI as thick fog engulfed parts of the Netherlands overnight.

The warning is for parts of Drenthe, Groningen and Overijssel, under the new regional weather warning system, which was first used on Saturday.

Fog consumed other areas over the weekend, including Utrecht, Noord-Brabant and parts of Gelderland and Zuid-Holland.

Two freight ships collided on the Maas river near Den Bosch on Saturday morning. No one was reported injured but one of the ships was badly damaged, according to Omroep Brabant.

The alert went out on Monday morning at 2am and will last until around 10am when the mist has cleared.

Road drivers are being warned to slow down and take more distance while driving. Fog reduces visibility to within 200 metres in certain places.
